name: MDS211 Lecture 28 New Professor Practice Set
subtitle: Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges · 20 Questions · Slide-Only, No Past-Paper Reliance
description: A dedicated 20-question set for Lecture 28 (Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges), built after a change of professor for this lecture. The slide content is unchanged, but since a new professor now writes the exam, this set avoids the past-paper archive entirely and is written only from the lecture slide deck itself, reaching into content not covered in any earlier SA2 material for this lecture. Each question has a single best answer among five options, with a full explanation covering both why the correct answer is right and the specific wrong-answer trap built into the distractors.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of total cardiac output does the brain normally receive?
questions.explanation: The brain normally receives approximately 15% of total cardiac output, despite making up only about 2% of total body weight — reflecting its very high metabolic demand. Common trap: It's easy to underestimate how disproportionately blood-hungry the brain is relative to its size, but 15% of cardiac output going to an organ this small is already a large figure — don't round it down toward the more modest-sounding 5%.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The two vertebral arteries fuse to form the single basilar artery at which anatomical level?
options: At the level of the foramen magnum
Within the cavernous sinus
The junction of the medulla and the pons
The junction of the medulla and the spinal cord
The junction of the pons and the midbrain
questions.explanation: The two vertebral arteries fuse to form the single basilar artery specifically at the junction between the medulla and the pons. Common trap: The foramen magnum (A) is where the vertebral arteries first ENTER the cranial cavity, not the more rostral level where they actually fuse together into the basilar artery.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The anterior communicating artery, a key component of the Circle of Willis, directly connects which two vessels?
options: The middle cerebral artery and the posterior cerebral artery
The internal carotid artery and the basilar artery directly
The two posterior cerebral arteries
The two vertebral arteries
The two anterior cerebral arteries
questions.explanation: The anterior communicating artery is the short vessel that directly connects the two anterior cerebral arteries across the midline, completing the anterior part of the Circle of Willis. Common trap: The posterior communicating artery (not listed as an option here, but a common source of confusion) is the vessel that connects the internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries — a completely different connection from the anterior communicating artery's role.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Among the named cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery, the callosomarginal artery supplies which territory?
options: The orbital and medial surface of the frontal lobe only
The choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle
The frontal pole exclusively
The medial surface of the parietal lobe and the precuneus only
The paracentral lobule (leg/foot cortex) and the cingulate gyrus
questions.explanation: The callosomarginal artery, a major branch of the ACA, supplies the paracentral lobule (the motor and sensory cortex representing the leg and foot) as well as the cingulate gyrus. Common trap: The pericallosal artery (the ACA's terminal branch) is the one that supplies the medial parietal lobe and precuneus (D) — a different, more posterior ACA branch from the callosomarginal artery being asked about here.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Among the named cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery, which branch's territory corresponds to the angular gyrus?
options: The angular artery
The orbitofrontal artery
The posterior parietal artery
The precentral artery
The postcentral artery
questions.explanation: The angular artery, a named cortical branch of the MCA, supplies the territory of the angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) — a region critical for tasks like reading and spatial cognition. Common trap: The posterior parietal artery (C) supplies the posterior parietal cortex more broadly, a neighboring but distinct territory from the angular gyrus specifically supplied by the angular artery.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Among the named branches of the posterior cerebral artery, which branch supplies the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampal formation?
options: The calcarine artery
The anterior temporal artery
The parieto-occipital artery
The posterior temporal artery
The thalamogeniculate artery
questions.explanation: The anterior temporal branch of the PCA supplies the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampal formation — relevant to the memory impairment seen in some PCA-territory strokes. Common trap: The calcarine artery (A) instead supplies the walls of the calcarine sulcus (primary visual cortex territory) — a completely different PCA branch from the one supplying medial temporal, memory-related structures.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The classic clinical syndrome from a lenticulostriate artery (Charcot's aneurysm territory) infarct in the internal capsule includes contralateral arm, leg, and lower-face paralysis with an upper motor neuron pattern of facial weakness. What distinguishes UMN facial weakness from LMN facial weakness in this syndrome?
options: The weakness is more severe in the upper face than the lower face
There is no facial involvement at all in this syndrome whatsoever
The entire face, including the forehead, is paralyzed identically to a lower motor neuron lesion
Only the eye is affected, with the mouth and forehead completely spared
The forehead is spared, since the upper face gets bilateral cortical innervation
questions.explanation: In this internal capsule (UMN) lesion, the forehead is spared — the patient can still wrinkle the forehead and close the eye on the affected side — because the upper face receives bilateral cortical (corticobulbar) innervation, while only the lower face is affected, since it receives predominantly contralateral innervation. Common trap: Option C describes an LMN (peripheral, e.g., Bell's palsy) pattern instead, where the ENTIRE face including the forehead is paralyzed — the whole point of recognizing ‘UMN facial palsy’ in this vascular syndrome is that the forehead is spared, the opposite of option C.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Cerebral arteries anastomose (interconnect) with neighboring vessels at which structural level, and with what characteristic vessel wall feature?
options: At the arteriole level, with a thin tunica media and less connective tissue
At the venule level exclusively
At the capillary level, with a thick, well-supported tunica media
At the level of the large named trunk arteries themselves, not their smaller branches
Cerebral arteries never anastomose with one another at any level
questions.explanation: Cerebral arteries anastomose with neighboring territories at the arteriole level, and are characterized by a comparatively thin tunica media with less supportive connective tissue than similarly-sized vessels elsewhere in the body. Common trap: “Cerebral arteries never anastomose” (E) is a common misconception — while cerebral anastomoses are less robust than in some other vascular beds (which is exactly why watershed/borderzone regions are vulnerable to hypoperfusion), genuine arteriole-level anastomoses do exist between the ACA, MCA, and PCA territories.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The border regions where the territories of the ACA, MCA, and PCA meet (for example, the medial frontal/parietal region where ACA and MCA territories abut) are clinically important because they are:
options: Exclusively supplied by the choroid plexus
The only regions of the brain with dual arterial and venous supply simultaneously
Completely immune to ischemia under any circumstance
The primary sites of CSF production
Watershed (borderzone) areas, particularly vulnerable to infarction during systemic hypotension
questions.explanation: The border regions between adjacent arterial territories (ACA-MCA-PCA anastomotic zones) are known as watershed or borderzone areas, and are particularly vulnerable to infarction during episodes of systemic hypotension, since they depend on the weakest, most distal collateral flow from each territory. Common trap: “Completely immune to ischemia” (C) is the opposite of the truth — watershed zones are specifically HIGH-RISK areas for a distinct pattern of ischemic injury (borderzone/watershed infarcts), precisely because of their marginal collateral blood supply.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly matches a type of cerebrovascular abnormality to its definition?
options: Aneurysm: a blockage of a vessel by a clot or air bubble that traveled from elsewhere in the body
Thrombosis/embolism: an abnormal tangle of vessels disrupting artery-vein connections
All three terms are functionally identical, with no meaningful distinction
Aneurysm: a bulge or ballooning in the wall of a blood vessel
Arteriovenous malformation: a bulge or ballooning in the wall of a blood vessel
questions.explanation: An aneurysm is a bulge or ballooning in the wall of a blood vessel; thrombosis/embolism is a blockage by a clot or air bubble that has traveled from elsewhere; an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is an abnormal tangle of vessels disrupting normal artery-vein connections. Common trap: Option A describes thrombosis/embolism, not an aneurysm — each of these three terms has its own specific, distinct definition, and it's easy to swap them under exam pressure.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The mnemonic ‘FAST’ is widely used for public recognition of stroke symptoms. What does the ‘T’ stand for?
options: Tremor of the affected limb
Tongue deviation to one side
Time (to call emergency services)
Tingling sensation in the extremities
Temperature elevation (fever)
questions.explanation: FAST stands for Face (drooping), Arm (weakness), Speech (difficulty), and Time (to call emergency services immediately) — a widely used public-health mnemonic for recognizing stroke symptoms and prompting urgent action. Common trap: Tongue deviation (B) is a genuine finding in some neurological exams (e.g., CN XII palsy), which can make it a tempting guess here, but the FAST mnemonic's ‘T’ is specifically about the urgency of TIME, not any particular physical exam finding.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Among the three cerebellar arteries, which one specifically supplies the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle?
options: None of the three cerebellar arteries supply any choroid plexus
The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)
All three cerebellar arteries supply the fourth ventricle choroid plexus equally
The superior cerebellar artery (SCA)
questions.explanation: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) specifically supplies the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle, in addition to the posteroinferior cerebellum and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Common trap: SCA and AICA (C, E) both supply cerebellar territory too, but the specific fourth ventricle choroid plexus supply is PICA's distinguishing feature among the three cerebellar arteries.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The posterior meningeal artery, which supplies the dura of the posterior cranial fossa, arises as a branch of which vessels?
options: The ascending pharyngeal, vertebral, and occipital arteries
The internal carotid artery directly
The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries
The maxillary artery only
The ophthalmic artery exclusively
questions.explanation: The posterior meningeal artery arises as a branch of the ascending pharyngeal, vertebral, and occipital arteries, supplying the dura of the posterior cranial fossa. Common trap: The maxillary artery (D) is the origin of the MIDDLE meningeal artery instead — a different meningeal artery supplying a different (middle, not posterior) cranial fossa region.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The dura mater's sensory (nerve) supply comes from branches of the trigeminal nerve, together with sensory fibers from which cervical spinal nerves — a fact that helps explain why some intracranial pathology can cause referred neck/occipital pain?
options: C7 and C8
C2 and C3
The dura mater has no sensory nerve supply at all
T1 and T2
L1 and L2
questions.explanation: The dura mater receives sensory innervation from trigeminal nerve branches together with sensory fibers from the C2 and C3 cervical spinal nerves — which helps explain why posterior fossa or upper cervical dural irritation can be perceived as occipital or neck pain. Common trap: “The dura mater has no sensory nerve supply” (C) is incorrect and would actually contradict a very common clinical phenomenon — headaches from meningeal irritation (e.g., meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage) are only possible because the dura IS richly innervated.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The falx cerebelli, one of the dural folds/septa, separates which structures and contains which venous sinus?
options: Separates the two lateral ventricles; contains the inferior sagittal sinus
Separates the cerebellar hemispheres; contains the occipital sinus
Separates the cerebral hemispheres; contains the superior sagittal sinus
Separates the pituitary gland from the hypothalamus; contains no sinus
Separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum; contains the transverse sinuses
questions.explanation: The falx cerebelli is a small dural fold that separates the two cerebellar hemispheres and contains the occipital sinus. Common trap: Option C describes the falx CEREBRI instead (separating the cerebral hemispheres, containing the superior sagittal sinus) — a much larger, different dural fold from the smaller falx cerebelli being asked about here.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The great cerebral vein (of Galen), which receives the internal cerebral veins and the basal vein of Rosenthal before draining into the straight sinus, is notable for having:
options: A completely rigid, cartilage-reinforced wall structure
The thickest walls of any vein in the cranial cavity
Valves identical in number and structure to peripheral limb veins
Very thin walls and no valves
Very thick, muscular walls with numerous one-way valves
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein of Galen, like other dural venous sinuses and major intracranial veins, has very thin walls and no valves — unlike many peripheral veins, which rely on valves to help direct blood flow against gravity. Common trap: Peripheral limb veins (C) do rely heavily on valves for one-way flow, which can make it tempting to assume the same applies intracranially — but intracranial venous drainage, including the great cerebral vein, is specifically valveless.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Under normal (non-pathological) conditions, is there a true, pre-existing epidural space between the dura mater and the inner table of the skull?
options: Yes, but only in the posterior cranial fossa
There is no dura mater covering the skull at all, only the arachnoid
No — the dura is normally adherent to the skull, with no true epidural space
Yes, a wide, fluid-filled epidural space is always present
Yes, but only during childhood, closing completely by adulthood
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions there is no true epidural space — the dura mater is adherent to the inner table of the skull. An epidural hematoma, by tearing a meningeal vessel and stripping the dura away from bone, is what actually CREATES the potential space that we then call ‘epidural.’ Common trap: It's easy to assume the epidural, subdural, and subarachnoid spaces are all equally ‘real,’ pre-existing anatomical spaces — but the epidural ‘space’ is specifically a potential space, only created pathologically, unlike the genuinely-present subarachnoid space.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: The middle cerebral artery's neglect syndrome (contralateral neglect, most prominent with non-dominant/right hemisphere lesions) is attributed to infarction of cortex supplying which Brodmann areas?
options: Area 17 (primary visual cortex)
Areas 41 and 42 (primary auditory cortex)
Areas 1, 2, and 3 (primary somatosensory cortex)
Areas 5 and 7 (posterior parietal cortex)
Areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area)
questions.explanation: MCA-territory neglect syndrome is attributed to infarction of the posterior parietal cortex, Brodmann areas 5 and 7, most prominent and long-lasting when the lesion is in the right (non-dominant) hemisphere. Common trap: Broca's area (D, areas 44/45) is also MCA territory and produces a real deficit (non-fluent aphasia) if damaged, but it is not the area responsible for neglect syndrome — a different MCA-territory cortical region (parietal areas 5/7) is responsible for that particular deficit.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke by underlying mechanism?
options: Ischemic stroke = vessel occlusion; hemorrhagic stroke = vessel rupture
Ischemic stroke results from vessel rupture; hemorrhagic stroke results from vessel occlusion
Both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke result from the identical underlying mechanism
Ischemic stroke only occurs in the venous system, never the arterial system
Hemorrhagic stroke cannot occur intracranially, only in peripheral vessels
questions.explanation: Ischemic stroke results from occlusion of a cerebral vessel (via atherosclerosis, thrombosis, or embolism), cutting off blood supply to brain tissue; hemorrhagic stroke results from rupture of a vessel (aneurysm rupture or AVM rupture), causing bleeding into or around brain tissue. Common trap: Option B reverses the two mechanisms entirely — keeping straight that ‘ischemic = blocked’ and ‘hemorrhagic = ruptured/bleeding’ is the core distinction being tested here.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges (New Set)
questions.stem: Risk factors explicitly listed in this course for ischemic stroke (via atherosclerosis, thrombosis, or embolism) include hypertension, diabetes, obesity, cardiac disease, and:
options: Excessive vitamin D intake
Regular moderate exercise
A diet high in leafy green vegetables
Neck injury or trauma
Living at high altitude permanently, with no other risk factors
questions.explanation: This course explicitly lists neck injury or trauma alongside hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and cardiac disease as risk factors contributing to ischemic stroke (relevant, for example, to trauma-associated arterial dissection). Common trap: Regular exercise and a vegetable-rich diet (B, C) are generally PROTECTIVE lifestyle factors against vascular disease, not risk factors — the opposite of what's being asked about here.
